title: Psalm 34: Taste and See That the LORD Is Good
summary: David praises the LORD for answering him and delivering him from all his fears, and invites others to magnify God with him. The second half turns into teaching: the fear of the LORD means guarding the tongue, turning from evil, and seeking peace, because the LORD is near the brokenhearted and delivers the righteous from all their troubles.
story: Psalm 34 follows the hymn of Psalm 33 with a personal thanksgiving that quickly becomes a lesson. The speaker has been in real danger and has been rescued, and he wants others to learn what he learned. It is a psalm of praise and a wisdom psalm at once, and it shows how the Psalter turns one person's rescue into instruction for the whole people. The New Testament quotes and echoes it more than once: Peter builds part of his first letter on it, and John sees one of its lines fulfilled at the cross.
historical:
The heading ties the psalm to the time David pretended to be insane before Abimelech, so that the king drove him away. The story is told in 1 Samuel 21:10-15, where David, fleeing Saul, goes to the Philistine city of Gath and fears its king, whom that chapter calls Achish. He scratches on the doors and lets saliva run down his beard, and the king sends him off. The difference in the king's name has several suggested explanations. Abimelech may have been a traditional title for Philistine rulers (a king of Gerar has that name in Genesis 20 and 26), much as Pharaoh was a title in Egypt. Others think the heading reflects a slip in the tradition, or a different line of transmission. Many scholars regard the heading as a later editor's link between the psalm and David's life rather than the poet's own note, and the psalm itself doesn't mention madness or Philistines.

If the heading is followed, the setting is around the late eleventh century BC, when David was an outlaw fleeing Saul. The psalm reads as the reflection of someone who survived by the narrowest margin and learned that God, not his own cleverness, saved him.
cultural:
The angel of the LORD in verse 7 is a figure who appears through the Old Testament as God's messenger, sometimes speaking as God himself (for example to Hagar in Genesis 16 and to Moses at the bush in Exodus 3). Here he encamps around the faithful like an army pitched around a city. The image of young lions going hungry in verse 10 draws on the fact that lions still roamed parts of the land in biblical times; even the strongest hunters can lack food, while those who seek God do not lack what is good.

The fear of the LORD, a key phrase in verses 7, 9, and 11, is the Old Testament's basic term for true religion: reverent awe that leads to obedience and trust. It is the beginning of wisdom in Proverbs. The call Come, children, listen to me in verse 11 is the voice of a wisdom teacher, the way a father or elder in Israel would instruct the young. Verse 20, which speaks of bones not being broken, echoes a detail in the law of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46).
literary: Psalm 34 is an acrostic: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. As in Psalm 25, one letter (waw) is missing and an extra verse beginning with pe closes the poem, so the pattern is slightly irregular. The acrostic form suggests completeness and also made the psalm easier to memorize and teach. The first half (verses 1 to 10) is thanksgiving, moving from I to us and inviting others in. The second half (verses 11 to 22) is instruction in the style of Proverbs. Refrains tie the halves together: the LORD delivers from all fears (verse 4), from all troubles (verses 6 and 17), from all afflictions (verse 19). The poem ends where it began, with those who take refuge in God.

outline.t: A vow to bless the LORD and an invitation to magnify him together
Taste and see: those who fear him lack nothing
A teacher's lesson in the fear of the LORD
The LORD's eyes on the righteous and nearness to the brokenhearted
Many afflictions, full deliverance, and redemption for his servants

doctrines.note: The second half teaches wisdom in its biblical sense: the fear of the LORD shown in how one speaks and acts. Good days come not from cleverness but from guarding the tongue, turning from evil, and pursuing peace.

The LORD watches, hears, encamps around, and delivers. The psalm doesn't promise the righteous an easy life; verse 19 says their afflictions are many. It promises that none of them is beyond God's reach.
Verse 18 says the LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the contrite in spirit. God's nearness is found not only after trouble ends but inside it.

words.note: Ta'am, to taste. In verse 8 the psalmist invites others to taste and see. The word is used literally of eating (Jonathan tasting honey in 1 Samuel 14) and figuratively of discernment. Its use here suggests that knowledge of God's goodness comes by experience, by trying and testing, not only by hearsay. Peter picks up this line in 1 Peter 2:3.

Yir'ah, fear. The fear of the LORD in verse 11 means reverence and awe that shape a life. It is not terror that drives a person away but a weight of respect that draws him to obey and trust. In verse 9 those who fear God lack nothing, which shows it as the root of security, not anxiety.

Shavar, to break. It appears twice with very different weight: God is near the brokenhearted, literally the broken of heart (verse 18), and not one of the righteous one's bones will be broken (verse 20). God comes close to the broken, and keeps the righteous from being finally broken.

christ: Peter quotes Psalm 34 twice in his first letter. He echoes verse 8 when he says believers have tasted that the Lord is good (1 Peter 2:3), and he quotes verses 12 to 16 at length (1 Peter 3:10-12) to teach suffering Christians how to live with enemies. In that first passage the Lord who is tasted is Christ. John reports that the soldiers didn't break Jesus' legs at the crucifixion and says this fulfilled the Scripture that not one of his bones would be broken (John 19:36). Many interpreters think John has in mind both the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46) and this psalm's promise about the righteous sufferer. Jesus is the righteous one whose afflictions were many and whom the LORD delivered from them all, finally through resurrection.

hard.q: Does the psalm promise that those who fear God will never lack anything or suffer harm?
hard.a: Verses 9 and 10 say those who fear the LORD lack nothing, and verse 20 says none of the righteous one's bones will be broken. Yet Scripture is full of faithful people who went hungry, were injured, or were killed, and the psalm itself admits in verse 19 that the afflictions of the righteous are many. Most interpreters read these lines as wisdom sayings, which state how God's world generally works and where it is finally heading, rather than as guarantees for every circumstance. Others stress that lack no good thing is measured by God's judgment of what is good, not ours. Christians add that the promise finds its full answer beyond death: Peter quotes this psalm to believers facing persecution, not to promise escape, but to assure them that God's eyes are on them and that their final rescue is secure.

questions: What is the difference between knowing about God's goodness and tasting it? Where have you tasted it?
Verses 13 and 14 focus on speech and peace. Which of those instructions is hardest for you right now?
The LORD is near to the brokenhearted. Who in your life is brokenhearted, and how might you share that promise with them without making it sound cheap?
